title: Zodiacal glow lightens Paranal sky
caption: Zodiacal light and the Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Toward the center left of this picture, the Milky Way, rich in nebulae, stars and gas clouds, rises above the Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope (VLT) at Paranal Observatory. On the right, a lovely, almost triangular band of diffuse light arcs above the horizon, competing for attention.

That band is zodiacal light. It lies along the ecliptic, the path the Sun appears to trace across our sky. The glow comes from sunlight scattered by dust in the space between the planets, spread through the plane of the Solar System.

Because it follows the ecliptic, the glow falls within the Zodiac, the band of sky that reaches eight degrees on either side of the ecliptic and holds the traditional zodiacal constellations. That is where the phenomenon gets its name.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to Y. Beletsky (LCO)/ESO. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: Zodiacal light is diffuse and faint, and a camera gathering light over time may show it more plainly than the eye would.
